# Car idles fine, but gas pedal doesn't do anything after failed jump start

When a vehicle starts perfectly yet refuses to accelerate, the issue is rarely mechanical damage to the pedals themselves. The physical linkage or electronic throttle body remains in the same state whether the engine was running on its own power or being forced by an external source. In your specific case involving the 2006 Toyota Camry LE, the symptoms point squarely at a loss of communication between the Engine Control Module (ECM) and the Powertrain Control Module (PCM), often colloquially referred to as the "computer brain" of the car.

The smoking jumper cables indicate that the initial battery connection was likely reversed or the voltage differential was too extreme for the internal capacitors, causing arcing. While you managed to start the car using a second jump source, the event almost certainly triggered a protective shutdown sequence within the vehicle's electronic architecture. Modern Toyotas of this era rely heavily on CAN bus communication for critical safety functions like the accelerator pedal position sensor (APP). If the system detects a voltage spike or a loss of reference ground during the high-current surge from the jumper cables, it may enter a "limp mode" to prevent catastrophic engine failure.

You asked if someone tampered with the fuse panel inside the cabin. It is highly unlikely that a neighbor accidentally blew a specific fuse for the accelerator pedal without affecting other electronics. The fuel pump, ignition coils, and idle air control valve are powered by different circuits. If those systems remain functional, the main power fuses are intact. The missing fuse cover you noticed is merely cosmetic; it does not confirm which circuit was affected. However, the absence of acceleration suggests a software lockout rather than a blown fuse for the throttle actuator.

To diagnose this without guessing, you need to verify the status of the Vehicle Speed Sensor (VSS) and the Throttle Position Sensor (TPS). The car can idle because the ECM is receiving a closed-throttle signal from the pedal sensor, telling it to maintain minimum RPM. When you press the pedal, the TPS should send an increasing voltage or digital count to the PCM. If the ECU detects that this signal didn't change despite physical input, it will cut fuel injection and spark timing immediately to protect the engine.

The most probable scenario here is that the ECM has latched a diagnostic trouble code (DTC) related to the accelerator pedal circuit. In many 2006 Camry models, a P1273 or P0120 series code indicates an open circuit or implausible signal in the throttle system. The car will start and idle because those codes might only be active when the driver requests load (acceleration). You cannot drive "again" safely until that code is cleared and the system re-learns its baseline parameters, which requires a specific reset procedure often involving disconnecting the battery for more than 15 minutes to fully drain the backup memory in the PCM.

Regarding your question about the neighbor's mistake: while their technique with the cables was dangerousâsmoking insulation suggests significant arcing that could have damaged wiring harnessesâthe resulting "bricked" state of the car is a standard electronic safety response, not necessarily permanent hardware destruction. The accelerator pedal itself has not broken; the computer controlling it is simply refusing to execute commands until it verifies the integrity of the input signal.

Before attempting a diagnostic scan, check the battery voltage again. A weak alternator or a partially discharged battery after the jump can cause voltage drops that mimic sensor failures. Ensure the battery is fully charged and stable. If the voltage holds steady and the pedal still feels unresponsive, you will need an OBDII scanner to read the specific codes stored in the ECM. Once the code is identified and cleared, the car may require a drive cycle to re-establish communication protocols on the CAN bus.
